summary: Defines a data transfer protocol for moving data between hosts on the ARPANET, written by a group of authors from MIT, UCLA, BBN, Rand, SRI, Harvard and UCSB. It updates RFC 114 and works with the file transfer protocol. It was replaced by RFC 264.

plainLanguage.summary: The delivery truck for data. It sets simple rules for how the box is packed and sent so many different computers can send things to each other.

subtitle: The original specification for breaking up network messages into labeled blocks for applications like file transfer and remote job entry.

tldr.problem: Different applications on the ARPANET needed to send data but had no common way to break it into pieces and mark them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 171 defines the Data Transfer Protocol with three transfer modes: indefinite bit stream, transparent block, and descriptor-count block. Each transaction starts with a type byte and carries data or control information. A handshake procedure lets both sides agree on which modes to use.
tldr.outcome: This RFC was replaced by RFC 264 in November 1971, which revised and clarified the protocol. It also updates RFC 114.

today: RFC 171 was replaced by RFC 264 in November 1971, which refined the protocol based on implementation feedback. Both are now historical, as the ARPANET evolved to use simpler protocols.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 171 defines the Data Transfer Protocol (DTP), a low-level mechanism for moving data between ARPANET hosts. DTP is designed to support many applications: file transfer, remote job entry, network mail, graphics, remote execution, and terminal communication. Unlike a full application protocol, DTP focuses only on how to separate messages into logical blocks (transactions), separate data from control information, and include basic error control. This separation allows applications to share DTP rather than each implementing their own transfer logic.
sections.plainLanguage: DTP is the common shipping system that all mail, files, and job programs can use without having to design their own way to send data.

sections.title: Three Transfer Modes and Flexibility
sections.content: DTP supports three ways to mark where one transaction ends and the next begins. Indefinite bit stream mode uses the connection closing as the end marker, useful for terminal links. Transparent block mode marks the end with a DLE (escape) sequence; any DLE in the data is doubled to avoid false ends. Descriptor-count mode includes a header with the byte count and sequence number. The protocol allows applications to mix these modes on the same connection, and permits implementations to support only a subset. A handshake procedure lets both sides advertise which receive modes they support.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to say where a chunk ends: when the plug is pulled, when you see a special stop signal, or by counting bytes. Both computers tell each other which ways they understand.

sections.title: Transaction Types and Control
sections.content: Every transaction starts with an 8-bit type byte. The protocol defines modes for data and control separately (types B0/B8 for bit stream, B1/B9 for transparent block, B2/BA for descriptor mode). It also defines control transactions for handshake (B3), information separators marking file/group/record/unit boundaries (B4), error codes (B5), abort signals (B6), and no-ops (B7). Sequence numbers in transactions help detect lost or out-of-order blocks. DTP does not dictate how to handle errors; the applications protocol defines what happens on failure.
sections.plainLanguage: Every block is labeled with what kind it is. Special labels mark where files end, where errors happened, or where to stop. The application decides what to do when something goes wrong.
